newsitem.title: ITALY: JOBS-Italy needs job market shakeout as EMU looms.
newsitem.headline: JOBS-Italy needs job market shakeout as EMU looms.

text.p: Italy is hell-bent on joining Europe's single currency club but the price could be lengthening dole queues unless radical steps are taken to shake up a hidebound labour market.

With more than 12 percent of the labour force out of work, Italy has an overall jobless rate above the EU average of 10.8 percent, but comparable to France and Germany which have been at the forefront of the drive to establish European currency union in 1999.

The headline jobless rate masks striking regional variations between the north, which in some areas enjoys virtually full employment, and parts of the poor south where up to half the labour force is officially out of work.

If Italy succeeds in its bid to join European economic and monetary union (EMU) the authorities will surrender control over the one lever which has traditionally got the economy out of a tight spot -- the exchange rate.
Deprived of the escape route given by periodic currency devaluations, Italy's exporters could come under strong pressure to reduce costs by shedding labour, economists say.

"Italy has one of the most rigid labour markets in Europe," said Salomon Brothers economist Jose Luis Alzola. "If they don't do something about it EMU could compound the unemployment problem if the country is hit by a powerful external shock."

A lingering fear is that Italy would struggle to cope with "asymmetric shock" -- one which hits some countries harder than others -- unless there is enough flexibility in the labour market allowing salary levels to adjust to changing conditions.
SHOCKS TO GUARD AGAINST

A jolt might come in the form of a slump in revenues from tourism -- which is key to the economies of southern Europe but less important in the north -- or a sharp fall in demand for subcompact cars, an Italian speciality.

"If you get an asymmetric shock you may get a situation in which central (European Union) monetary policy would not be able to respond to a problem in a specific country," said Alzola. "You should have a flexible labour market to adjust to such an unwelcome shock."

If Italy fails to loosen its jobs market in the years ahead unemployment could soar, particularly if productivity growth lags that of other EMU countries without a downward adjustment in wages to compensate, economists say.
That could cause the budget deficit to balloon as the cost of unemployment benefit rises.
High among the list of priorities for the reformers is a move away from centralised bargaining under which nationwide contracts are negotiated between unions and employers.
The preferred option is a system of wage deals which reflects productivity in individual offices and factories.
"Salaries must be linked to productivity levels and trends," Deputy Prime Minister Walter Veltroni said recently.
Bank of Italy governor Antonio Fazio has repeatedly sounded warnings over the need for increased wage flexibility as Italy gears up for the monetary rigours of EMU membership.

"In Italy and other industrial economies cyclical and structural unemployment derives from the rigidity, in each company, of the overall salary bill, even when faced with negative trends in global demand and in revenues," said Fazio in a recent speech.

Small companies employing less than 20 people created 1.3 million new jobs between 1981 and 1991, reflecting greater freedom of employers to set salaries, while employee numbers in larger firms rose by just 100,000 over the same period, he said.
Employee numbers in small companies were hit by a jobs shakeout affecting the entire economy in the early 1990s but have since started to climb steeply, he said.
The success of Italy's celebrated small, family-owned companies "is also the fruit of more cooperative industrial relations in the management of working hours and in setting salaries," said Fazio.
Small and medium-sized firms pay salaries which are on average one-fifth lower than those offered by larger companies.
Italy's powerful unions have until recently strenuously opposed efforts by employers to restore regional wage variations which were prevalent in the 1950s under a system known as "salary cages".
CHANGE LOOMING?
There are signs that the mood could be changing.

"I agree with governor Fazio. Salaries have to be flexible. I agree with the principle," said Sergio D'Antoni, secretary general of the catholic-inspired CISL union confederation in a recent interview with Milan newspaper Corriere della Sera.
One of the keys to easing the southern jobs crisis in the Mezzogiorno lies in increased salary flexibility.

Employers are currently bound by the nationwide labour contracts to apply similar wages in the south, where productivity generally lags behind the more efficient north, to those paid in the rest of the country.

"In the south you have a less qualified labour force, there is no mobility but people have to be paid the same wage as in the north," said Giovanna Mossetti, an economist with Milan-based brokerage firm Caboto.

Many small businesses in the south have got round the problem by illegally hiring casual labour at low salaries who are not registered as officially employed and therefore receive no social security benefits.
